- regola del capitolo: *"hold the test"*.
- 4 item formativi in coda; sommativo "Catch the overfitter" negli ultimi ~10′.

## *Fits the seen; misses the unseen.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-04_02.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce: train error = aderenza ai già-visti, non comportamento sui nuovi. È la pushback del cap. 02 (Clinician A, item 04) che torna a chiedere conto.
:::

## What does training error actually measure?

**Training error** = how well the model fits *the data it was trained on*.

It does **not** tell us how the model will do on patients we have not measured.

The more *flexible* the model, the better it can fit any specific training set — at the cost of fitting *that one set* rather than the underlying pattern.

::: {.notes}
Overfitting concettuale prima di nominarlo. Gancio cap. 02 item 04 ("but on a different group of patients?"): stessa domanda, oggi la chiudiamo.
:::

<!-- BEAT 3 — Sfida / U-curve -->

## *Training error falls. New-data error eventually rises.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-04_03.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
Punto chiave: la U. Train scende verso zero; new-data scende, minimo, poi risale; il gap si allarga oltre il minimo. Overfitting = impara il campione, non il segnale.
:::

## Overfitting — the signature

A model is **overfitting** when:

- its **training error is low** (it has memorised the training sample), **and**
- its **error on new data is much higher** (the gap is large).

It has captured *idiosyncrasies of the sample*, not the underlying signal.

The opposite failure — *underfitting* — is when **both** errors are *high*: the model is too rigid to capture even the training data.

::: {.notes}
Insisti sulla diagnosi differenziale: overfit = basso train + grande gap; underfit = entrambi alti e vicini. Item 01 testa proprio questo.
:::

<!-- ASIDE — what does "error" actually mean? threshold-based metrics + threshold-free metrics -->

## Aside — *Which* error? A quick metric tour {.smaller}

For a binary classifier, the **confusion matrix** counts four outcomes:

|  | predicted $+$ | predicted $-$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **actual $+$** | TP | FN |
| **actual $-$** | FP | TN |

From it, the most-used metrics:

- **Accuracy** $= \dfrac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$ — overall correct rate.
- **Balanced accuracy** $= \dfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\dfrac{TP}{TP + FN} + \dfrac{TN}{TN + FP}\right)$ — avoids the *majority-class trap* on imbalanced data.
- **Sensitivity** (recall, TPR) $= \dfrac{TP}{TP + FN}$ — of the actual positives, how many caught.
- **Specificity** (TNR) $= \dfrac{TN}{TN + FP}$ — of the actual negatives, how many spared.
- **Precision** (PPV) $= \dfrac{TP}{TP + FP}$ — of those flagged positive, how many really are.

::: {.notes}
Aside metriche — ~60-90″, non valutata.

- a voce: malattia rara al $5\%$, "sempre sano" → accuracy $95\%$ ma sensitivity $0$. Balanced accuracy neutralizza il bias di prevalenza.
- sinonimi: sensitivity ↔ recall; precision ↔ PPV (clinico vs ML).
- gancio: tutte presuppongono una soglia fissa — slide dopo la togliamo.
:::

## Aside — Threshold-free: AUC-ROC vs AUC-PR

Most classifiers output a **score** (often a probability); the threshold turns it into a label. Sweeping the threshold traces two curves:

- **ROC curve** — sensitivity vs $1 - \text{specificity}$ across thresholds. Its area, **AUC-ROC** $\in [0.5, 1]$, is the probability that a random positive scores higher than a random negative.
- **PR curve** — precision vs recall. Its area, **AUC-PR**, is more informative when the **positive class is rare**.

Rule of thumb: **AUC-ROC** when classes are roughly balanced; **AUC-PR** under heavy imbalance (rare disease, fraud, anomaly detection).

::: {.notes}
Threshold-free — ~60-90″. Idea: buona metrica = non dipende da una soglia, riassume tutte.

- a voce: AUC-PR baseline = prevalenza (non $0.5$); ROC può sembrare alta ($0.85$+) con pochi veri positivi tra molti falsi → screening malattie rare, usa AUC-PR.
- nominale e basta; dettagli in `index-full.Rmd`.
:::

<!-- BEAT 4 — Nodo: contamination principle -->

## *Every decision spends data.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-04_04.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Regola del capitolo: contamination principle. Ogni numero usato per scegliere è speso, non è più stima onesta. Per questo il test sta dietro vetro fino a scelta fatta.
:::

## The contamination principle

> Every time you take a decision based on a number from a dataset, **that number is no longer a valid estimate**.

Concretely:

- Use validation error to *choose* between models → that validation error is **spent** as a future estimate.
- Use test error to *choose* (even just to pick a winner among candidates) → the test set is **spent**.

The only honest number is one *that was not used to decide anything*.

::: {.notes}
Lente che unifica train/val/test. Lo studente sa che serve un test; la sottigliezza è il *perché*: ogni decisione costa un numero.

- frase da incidere: *"every decision after looking at a number contaminates that number as a future estimate"*.
- vocabolario richiamato al sommativo.
:::

<!-- BEAT 5 — Metodo: 3-way split + K-fold CV (perno del sommativo) -->

## *Three sets, one job each — and the test stays untouched.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-04_05.png){fig-align="center" width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
Tre set: train fitta, validation ($K$-fold CV) sceglie, test conferma. Perno del capitolo: anticipa la tabella a 4 righe del sommativo ($M_A$–$M_D$, train vs CV).
:::

## Train / Validation / Test — one role each

| Subset | Role | Used to |
|---|---|---|
| **Training** | fit | learn the model's parameters |
| **Validation** | choose | compare candidate models / hyperparameter settings |
| **Test** | confirm | estimate final performance on truly unseen data |

The same data **cannot** play two roles. Choosing a model on a set spends that set's number as a future estimate.

::: {.notes}
A voce il *perché* tre e non due: fittare + scegliere (consuma il set) + un set intatto per stimare. Richiama la contamination rule del beat prima.
:::

## $K$-fold cross-validation — the recipe

The validation step, done practically:

1. Split the (non-test) data into **$K$ equal blocks**.
2. For $k = 1, \ldots, K$: train on the other $K - 1$ blocks; estimate error on block $k$.
3. **Average** the $K$ per-fold error rates → the **CV error**.

**Standard $K \in [5, 10]$:** smaller $K$ trains on less data (high bias); larger $K$ has smaller folds (high variance).

The CV error **estimates** the prediction error of the chosen model on *unseen* patients.

::: {.notes}
Procedura canonica del validation. Dopo la scelta col CV quel numero è speso → pushback item 03 + sommativo. La regola sui $K$ è bias-variance dei fold: voce docente, non valutato.
:::

<!-- ASIDE — once the model is validated: what did it learn? global (VIMP) + local (SHAP) -->

## Aside — What did the model *learn*? Global importance (VIMP)

After validating *that* a model predicts well, a second question follows: **which features is it relying on?**

**Variable importance — permutation-based (VIMP):**

1. Measure the validated model's error $E$.
2. **Permute** the values of feature $X_j$ across patients — this breaks any signal in $X_j$, keeping everything else fixed.
3. Re-measure the error $E_j$. The **importance of $X_j$** is $E_j - E$: how much performance *drops* when $X_j$ is scrambled.

Born with **random forests**, but works for *any* fitted model (**model-agnostic**).

::: {.notes}
VIMP — ~60″. Idea: permuti $X_j$, se l'errore non cambia non contribuisce. Globale: una classifica per l'intero dataset.

- caveat a voce: NON è causalità — può pescare confondenti (es. "ICU room number" proxy di gravità).
- predittori correlati: l'importanza si "spalma", sottostima entrambi.
- vendila come sanity check post-fit, non spiegazione causale.
:::

## Aside — Why *this* prediction? Local explanations (SHAP)

VIMP tells you *which features matter on average*. **SHAP** tells you *how each feature contributed to a single patient's prediction*.

- Borrowed from cooperative **game theory** (Shapley values, 1953): each feature is a "player"; its SHAP value is its **fair share** of the prediction's deviation from the average.
- For one patient: a positive SHAP value pushes the prediction *up*; a negative one pushes it *down*. Contributions are **additive**.
- Aggregated across patients, SHAP also yields a *global* view that is consistent with the local explanations.

Model-agnostic; standard tooling for tree ensembles, deep nets, and LLMs.

::: {.notes}
SHAP — ~60″. Idea: scomposizione additiva per-paziente → *"why was THIS patient flagged?"*.

- onestà: spiega il modello, non la biologia (come combina le feature, non perché la malattia esista).
- take-home: VIMP globale + SHAP locale = i due bisogni clinici.
- gancio cap. 05: nei deep net SHAP resta utile ma più costoso.
:::

## Pre-hook → chapter 5: deep learning

You now have a discipline that works for *any* classifier you can build: fit, cross-validate, hold out a test set, report the honest number.

But what if the **model itself** can be made arbitrarily complex — a network of millions of artificial *neurons* that can, in principle, fit *anything*?

The cross-validation discipline still holds. But the *architecture* of the model becomes a new question. **Deep neural networks** — next.

::: {.notes}
Pre-hook cap. 05. La disciplina sopravvive, anzi conta di più. Nuovo asse di scelta: non più quale algoritmo/hyperparametro ma quale architettura. Lascia aperto *neurons + layers* senza il meccanismo (backprop): è il gancio.
:::

<!-- Item 01 — MCQ — Diagnose overfitting -->

## Item 01 — Question {.smaller}

Four classifiers evaluated on the same task with **5-fold CV**:

| Classifier | Training error | CV error |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $M_1$ | $25\%$ | $28\%$ |
| $M_2$ | $0\%$  | $32\%$ |
| $M_3$ | $48\%$ | $50\%$ |
| $M_4$ | $7\%$  | $9\%$  |

Which **one** shows the clearest signature of **overfitting**?

- **A)** $M_1$ &nbsp;·&nbsp; **B)** $M_2$ &nbsp;·&nbsp; **C)** $M_3$ &nbsp;·&nbsp; **D)** $M_4$

::: {.notes}
Item 01 — Comprehension / MCQ / low-med. Obj. 1 (diagnose overfitting).

- distrattore D pesca il misconception "basso training = overfit": serve basso train + grande gap.
- file: `course/04-model-selection/items/item_01_diagnose-overfitting_mcq.md`.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Lascia 60s. Misconception frequente: scegliere C ($M_3$) per "errore alto = sbagliato" → è underfitting. Regola: guarda prima il *gap*.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution

**Correct: B — $M_2$.**

The overfitting signature: **low training error + much higher error on new data** (large gap). $M_2$ has $0\%$ training error but $32\%$ CV — memorised the sample, not the signal.

Why the distractors are wrong:

- **A** ($M_1$, $25/28\%$) — no overfit: small gap, both moderate.
- **C** ($M_3$, $48/50\%$) — **underfitting** (the opposite): both errors high and near chance. Model too rigid.
- **D** ($M_4$, $7/9\%$) — **healthy fit**: both low and close. *Low training error alone is not overfit.*

::: {.notes}
Discriminante: gap grande + train basso. Non errore alto generico (underfit), non train basso da solo (healthy).
:::

<!-- Item 02 — Applicativa — Compute K-fold CV -->

## Item 02 — Question {.smaller}

A classifier evaluated on $20$ patients with **5-fold CV** (4 patients per fold):

| Fold | Misclassified | Out of | Per-fold error |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | 1 | 4 | $25\%$ |
| 2 | 1 | 4 | $25\%$ |
| 3 | 2 | 4 | $50\%$ |
| 4 | 0 | 4 | $0\%$  |
| 5 | 2 | 4 | $50\%$ |

1. **Compute** the 5-fold CV error rate. Show your formula.
2. **State** what number the CV error rate *estimates* (1–2 sentences).
3. **Describe** what would change with $K = 10$ on the same 20 patients: (a) the procedure, (b) one trade-off.

::: {.notes}
Item 02 — Application / applicativa / medium. Obj. 3 (calcolo $K$-fold CV + cosa stima + trade-off $K$). Rubrica: `course/04-model-selection/rubriche/rubrica_02_compute-kfold-cv.md`.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca per i calcoli. Risposta crib: CV $= (25+25+50+0+50)/5 = 30\%$ (o $6/20$). Punto chiave: la CV error stima la prediction error sui non-visti, NON train, NON test.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution {.smaller}

**1.** CV error = average of per-fold rates:
$$\text{CV error} = \frac{25\% + 25\% + 50\% + 0\% + 50\%}{5} = 30\%.$$
Equivalent: $(1+1+2+0+2)/20 = 6/20 = 30\%$.

**2.** It **estimates the prediction error of the classifier on unseen patients** drawn from the same population. *Not* the training error (fit on seen data), *not yet* the test error (reserved for after the choice).

**3.** With **$K = 10$** on the same 20 patients:

- **(a)** $10$ folds of $2$ patients each; train on $18$, estimate on $2$, average the $10$ rates.
- **(b)** Trade-off: more training data per fold → less bias *but* smaller folds → noisier per-fold rates → more variance. Standard $K \in [5, 10]$ balances both.

::: {.notes}
A voce: CV error è stima onesta *solo se non ancora usata per scegliere*. Quella usata per la scelta = lo spent number dell'item 03.
:::

<!-- Item 03 — MCQ — After CV: next step -->

## Item 03 — Question {.smaller}

A team uses **5-fold CV** on training+validation to compare four candidates ($M_A, M_B, M_C, M_D$). **$M_B$** wins with CV error $18\%$. They have a separate **test set** untouched since day 1. What is the **correct next step**?

- **A)** Report $M_B$'s CV error ($18\%$) as expected performance on new patients — no further evaluation needed.
- **B)** Retrain $M_B$ on train+val combined; evaluate **once** on the held-out test set; report that test error.
- **C)** Re-run 5-fold CV with $K = 10$ to confirm the $18\%$; then report it.
- **D)** Pool train+val+test into one combined dataset; report $M_B$'s average error on the pool.

::: {.notes}
Item 03 — Application / MCQ / medium. Obj. 2 (contamination dopo un vincitore CV).

- A: distrattore più attraente — sembra performance, ma è già spent nella scelta.
- D: il più dannoso — contamina il test come training.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Lascia 60-90s. Se esitano tra A e B, richiama la contamination rule. A è sbagliato: $18\%$ ha scelto $M_B$ tra quattro → ottimisticamente biased.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution {.smaller}

**Correct: B.** $M_B$'s CV error ($18\%$) is the very number that *chose* $M_B$ among four candidates. By the **contamination principle**, that number is no longer unbiased — it is *optimistically biased* (the smallest of four CV errors). The **test set** is the only untouched dataset.

Why the distractors are wrong:

- **A** — classic contamination violation. $18\%$ has been spent.
- **C** — re-running CV doubles down on the same set; the test set remains the only fresh source.
- **D** — uses the test set as training data, destroying its role. Worst of all.

::: {.notes}
Domanda discriminante: *"is there a dataset not yet used in any decision about $M_B$?"* → solo B. Il test serve una volta sola, dopo tutte le scelte.
:::

<!-- Item 04 — Argomentativa — Cross-technique trap -->

## Item 04 — Question {.smaller}

A colleague compares **3 ML techniques** ($k$-NN, SVM-kernel, RF), each with its own hyperparameters. Their procedure:

| Day | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Split: train + validation + **test** (locked away on day 1). |
| 2 | For each technique, use 5-fold CV on train+val to tune its hyperparameters. |
| 3 | Retrain each tuned candidate on train+val combined. |
| 4 | Evaluate the 3 candidates on the **test set**; record each one's test error. |
| 5 | Pick the technique with the **lowest test error**; report that test error. |

*"Each technique was tuned correctly with CV. Test set was never touched during training. What could be wrong?"*

1. **Find the exact flaw**: where (and *how*) is the contamination principle violated?
2. **Propose the correct procedure** and explain why it has no flaw.

::: {.notes}
Item 04 — Argumentation / medium-high. Obj. 1 + 2 (cross-technique trap).

- punto sottile: la *seconda* selezione (passo 4–5) avviene sul test set.
- soglia: C1 *e* C2 a Base. Rubrica: `course/04-model-selection/rubriche/rubrica_04_skip-the-test-critique.md`.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca, ragionamento in 2 parti. Argomentativo alto: lo studente sente che "qualcosa non quadra" ma non nomina la *seconda selezione*. Costruisci: validation sceglie tra modelli = anche tra tecniche.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution {.smaller}

**1. Flaw at Steps 4–5.** The test set has been used to *choose* among the three retrained techniques. Picking the technique with the lowest test error among three is a **decision based on test-set numbers** — the contamination principle rules it out. The reported test error of the winner $M_\star$ is no longer unbiased: it is **the minimum of three test errors**, optimistically biased. Each technique's *within-technique* CV tuning at Step 2 was correct, but a **second selection step** has been hidden inside Steps 4–5, turning the test set into a *between-technique validation set*.

**2. Correct procedure.** Do **all** selection at the validation step — both within and between techniques:

- For each technique, CV-tune its hyperparameters on train+val.
- **Use the same CV to compare the 3 tuned candidates** and pick a single $M_\star$ (the technique-and-setting with lowest CV error overall).
- Retrain only $M_\star$ on train+val combined.
- Evaluate $M_\star$ **once** on the held-out test set; report.

When the test set is consulted, no decision is open: it is used *purely* to estimate.

::: {.notes}
Bonus a voce: la fix non è "più partizioni" ma disciplina — un quarto set subirebbe lo stesso problema. Regola: tutte le selezioni sulla validation, una sola valutazione sul test.

- grading: item più sottile finora → premia la coerenza del ragionamento più del vocabolario.
:::

<!-- Summative -->

## Summative — *Catch the overfitter* {.inverse .smaller background-color="#1F4257"}

Four $k$-NN candidates ($k = 1, 5, 15, 51$) tuned on $100$ patients with 5-fold CV:

| Model | $k$ | Training error | 5-fold CV error |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $M_A$ | 1 | $0 / 100$ ($0\%$) | $30 / 100$ ($30\%$) |
| $M_B$ | 5 | $12 / 100$ ($12\%$) | $18 / 100$ ($18\%$) |
| $M_C$ | 15 | $20 / 100$ ($20\%$) | $22 / 100$ ($22\%$) |
| $M_D$ | 51 | $40 / 100$ ($40\%$) | $42 / 100$ ($42\%$) |

For each group:

1. **Identify the overfitter** and say *why* (which signature?).
2. **Pick the winner** by CV error.
3. *Why* is the winner's CV error **not** a trustworthy estimate of its performance on new patients? What data would you use?
4. Assign the three subsets: **training** is used to ___, **validation (5-fold CV)** is used to ___, **test** is used to ___.

::: {.notes}
Sommativo — ultimi ~10′ (min 20-30). Tempi: ~2′ leggi+assegna · ~5′ riempi (foto upload *durante*) · ~3′ reveal.

- Slido poll: overfitter id (4 opzioni $M_A$/$M_B$/$M_C$/$M_D$).
- duale: tabella + 4 risposte di gruppo nel doc condiviso.
- reveal cap. 02-03: *"this is what was at stake when Clinician A asked us in ch. 02 'but on a different group?' — and this is why $1$NN's paper-thin wrap in ch. 03 was a trap."*
:::

## Summative — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca, 4 risposte di gruppo sulla shared board. Teachable moment: chi pick $M_C$ "per il gap più piccolo" ha letto male il criterio (è lowest CV, non smallest gap) — non penalizzare, usa per il reveal.
:::

## Summative — Solution {.smaller}

**1. Overfitter: $M_A$.** Signature: $0\%$ training + $30\%$ CV (30-point gap). $k=1$ memorises every training point — perfect on training, bad on new patients.

**2. Winner by CV: $M_B$ ($18\%$).** Lowest CV error.

**3. The CV error has been *used to choose* $M_B$ among four candidates.** Contamination principle: that number is now optimistically biased, not unbiased. Use the **separate held-out test set** (untouched in selection) to get a trustworthy number.

**4. Roles:**

| Subset | Used to |
|:-:|:--|
| **TRAINING** | fit the model's parameters |
| **VALIDATION** (5-fold CV) | choose among candidate models / hyperparameters |
| **TEST** | estimate final performance on truly unseen patients |

*Take-home:* this chapter's discipline answers both prior cliff-hangers — *"but on a different group of patients?"* (ch. 02) and the $1$NN paper-thin wrap (ch. 03). The architecture question opens at chapter 5.

::: {.notes}
Reveal pedagogico:

- $M_D$ ($k=51$) = underfit, train alto perché troppo rigido. Chiedi "perché alto sia su train sia in CV?" → apre il bias-variance.
- $M_C$: no gap ma non vince — assenza di overfit non basta.
- pre-hook ch. 05 nelle ultime righe.
:::
